title: Einstein and Bohr Argue for Thirty Years
text:
Albert Einstein and Niels Bohr met in Berlin in 1920 and liked each other at once. Einstein wrote to Bohr afterward that few people had ever given him such joy simply by being present.

Then quantum mechanics divided them. Bohr believed the new theory was complete: at the smallest scale, nature was governed by probability, and some questions had no definite answer until a measurement was made. Einstein could not accept that physics would end with chance.

At the Solvay Conference in Brussels in 1927, the debate became legendary. At breakfast Einstein would propose a clever thought experiment that seemed to break the theory. Bohr would worry over it all day, and by dinner he usually had an answer. In 1930 Einstein proposed a box that released light at a precise moment. Bohr spent a sleepless night and then showed that Einstein's own theory of general relativity saved quantum mechanics.

The argument never ended. In 1949 Bohr wrote a long, warm essay describing their discussions. They remained friends until Einstein died in 1955. When Bohr died in 1962, the last drawing on the blackboard in his study was reportedly a sketch of Einstein's light box.
lesson: You can disagree with someone deeply and for years while keeping respect and affection. A worthy opponent sharpens your thinking more than an easy ally.
source: Niels Bohr, "Discussion with Einstein on Epistemological Problems in Atomic Physics," in Albert Einstein: Philosopher-Scientist, ed. P. A. Schilpp (1949)
